            fontsize=6.5, fontweight='bold', linespacing=1.1)

ax.plot([grid_left, grid_right], [grid_top, grid_top], color='#999999', linewidth=1.0)

    ax.plot([bx, bx + 0.08], [y1, y1], color='#CCCCCC', linewidth=0.8)

# Operating Range
or_x = grid_right + 0.15
ax.text(or_x + 0.55, grid_top - 0.06, 'Operating\nRange', ha='center', va='bottom',
        fontsize=6.5, fontweight='bold', linespacing=1.1)
for i, sig in enumerate(signals):

    ax.text(or_x, y, op_range[sig], ha='left', va='center', fontsize=6.5,

for label, color in items:
    rect = patches.Rectangle((lx, ly), 0.16, 0.13, facecolor=color,
                              edgecolor='#AAAAAA', linewidth=0.5)
    ax.add_patch(rect)
    ax.text(lx + 0.21, ly + 0.065, label, ha='left', va='center',
            fontsize=5.5, color='#555555')
    lx += 1.02

# Title
ax.text(3.375, 0.18, 'Signal Taxonomy: Effectiveness Across Evaluation Dimensions',
        ha='center', va='center', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
ax.text(3.375, 0.42, 'Color intensity encodes magnitude; classification from monotonicity analysis',

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic empirical analysis of training dynamic signals as model collapse severity monitors.
Through controlled iterative retraining experiments on Qwen2.5-0.5B with WikiText-2 across three contamination levels and five generational depths, we established three main findings.
First, spectral signals (stable rank, spectral entropy) and output signals (token entropy, perplexity) maintain monotonic ordering with contamination severity, with effect sizes spanning orders of magnitude: $6.6\times$ stable rank separation and $53\times$ perplexity divergence at full contamination (source: \texttt{mvp\_frac50\_100}).
Second, stable rank deviation reaches 34.4\% at just 3\% of training progress, providing early warning before catastrophic degradation materializes (source: \texttt{within\_gen\_analysis}).
Third, not all signals are equally trustworthy: gradient norms are non-monotonic under QLoRA, downstream benchmarks are insensitive at small scale, and per-layer analysis reveals sub-module bifurcation invisible to aggregate metrics (source: \texttt{per\_layer\_analysis\_v5}).
Together, these findings yield a practitioner-oriented signal taxonomy that specifies which signals to trust, when, and at what granularity.

\paragraph{Broader impact.}
As LLM-generated text becomes increasingly prevalent in training corpora---through web scraping, synthetic data augmentation, and iterative self-improvement---the risk of undetected model collapse grows.
Our work contributes to AI safety by demonstrating that collapse leaves detectable fingerprints in standard training signals, well before it manifests in downstream benchmarks or human evaluation.
The monitoring signals we evaluate are computationally free (output signals) or near-free (spectral signals via periodic SVD), require no external reference distribution, and can be integrated into existing training pipelines with minimal engineering effort.
Making collapse visible during training---rather than discovering it post-hoc---enables practitioners to intervene before degradation becomes irreversible.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Several extensions would strengthen and broaden these findings.

Third, broader collapse sources: evaluating signal behavior under distribution shift, data poisoning, and mixed-provenance synthetic data would test whether our taxonomy generalizes beyond the iterative self-generation setting.

Evaluation perplexity, computed on clean held-out data, reliably tracks severity \emph{across} generations but achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.534$ for within-generation collapse detection---indistinguishable from random chance.
A practitioner watching only perplexity would have no warning that collapse is underway until the next generation of synthetic data has already been produced.

Existing work addresses model collapse from two directions.
On the theoretical side, \citet{Shumailov2024} established the phenomenon, \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved that any nonzero synthetic fraction eventually induces strong collapse, and \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed that collapse alters neural scaling laws.

Missing from this landscape is a systematic analysis of which \emph{training-time signals} best track collapse severity, when they provide early warning, and where they saturate or actively mislead.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} highlight that even the definition of collapse varies across studies, further motivating signal-level analysis grounded in controlled experiments.

Neither provides a cross-family comparison of signal operating ranges or quantitative within-generation early warning thresholds.

We conduct a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as collapse severity monitors.
We evaluate four signal families---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (evaluation perplexity, token entropy, training loss), gradient (L2 norm), and downstream (HellaSwag accuracy)---across five experimental configurations spanning model scales (0.5B to 3B), fine-tuning methods (QLoRA and full fine-tuning), contamination fractions ($\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$), and text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed).

    These findings motivate a three-tier recommendation: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.
\end{enumerate}

Section~\ref{sec:method} details our iterative contamination protocol, signal definitions, and evaluation framework.
Section~\ref{sec:results} presents signal--severity correlations, within-generation early warning analysis, and the method-dependent signal taxonomy.

% Introduction — collapse_severity_monitor
% Data sources: plan006 (3-seed Cohen's d), within_gen_analysis, plan003-fullft-05B

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

As LLM-generated text pervades web-scraped training corpora, practitioners increasingly fine-tune models on data shaped by prior model generations.
This recursive dynamic creates self-consuming loops that cause \emph{model collapse}---progressive loss of distribution tails, contraction of output diversity, and degradation of acquired knowledge~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
The problem compounds: even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse at sufficient depth~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors accumulating across iterations at accelerating rates~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}.
Yet the metrics practitioners most commonly watch during training fail to detect this degradation within a run.
Training perplexity can \emph{decrease} as a model collapses, since it measures fit to data that is itself partially synthetic.
Evaluation perplexity, computed on clean held-out data, reliably tracks severity \emph{across} generations but achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.534$ for within-generation collapse detection---indistinguishable from random chance.
A practitioner watching only perplexity would have no warning that collapse is underway until the next generation of synthetic data has already been produced.

Existing work addresses model collapse from two directions.
On the theoretical side, \citet{Shumailov2024} established the phenomenon, \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved that any nonzero synthetic fraction eventually induces strong collapse, and \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed that collapse alters neural scaling laws.
On the mitigation side, data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, and verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025} each reduce collapse pressure under specific conditions.
Missing from this landscape is a systematic analysis of which \emph{training-time signals} best track collapse severity, when they provide early warning, and where they saturate or actively mislead.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} highlight that even the definition of collapse varies across studies, further motivating signal-level analysis grounded in controlled experiments.
The two closest concurrent works---SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026}, which monitors output embedding spectra, and the topological index of \citet{Kalinowski2026}---each address part of this gap but carry limitations: SIGMA requires a clean reference distribution and operates post-hoc; topological monitoring incurs higher computational cost.
Neither provides a cross-family comparison of signal operating ranges or quantitative within-generation early warning thresholds.

We conduct a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as collapse severity monitors.
We evaluate four signal families---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (evaluation perplexity, token entropy, training loss), gradient (L2 norm), and downstream (HellaSwag accuracy)---across five experimental configurations spanning model scales (0.5B to 3B), fine-tuning methods (QLoRA and full fine-tuning), contamination fractions ($\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$), and text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed).
Our central finding is that different signal families have complementary operating ranges, and the same signal's utility can flip from informative to misleading depending on the training method.

Our contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Signal--severity correlation.}
    Spectral and output signals track collapse across contamination levels.
    Spectral entropy achieves the largest effect size (Cohen's $d = 33.48$, coefficient of variation $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
    Validated across QLoRA and full fine-tuning, six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change regardless of training method.
    The exception---gradient norm, which is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning---demonstrates that method-dependence is a first-order concern for monitoring pipeline design.

    \item \textbf{Within-generation early warning and negative results.}
    Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.984$ at 10\% training progress for binary collapse detection, with 34.4\% deviation from baseline at 3\% of training.
    Training loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$).
    We document two negative results: evaluation perplexity achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.534$ for within-generation detection---the most commonly available metric fails at the most actionable task---and token entropy achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$, providing no reliable discrimination despite a large initial deviation.
    These failures have a structural explanation: evaluation perplexity accumulates degradation through the iterative contamination loop, not within a single generation's training, while token entropy's per-position measurement lacks the representational sensitivity of spectral signals.

    \item \textbf{Signal taxonomy with method-dependent operating ranges.}
    Signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale.
    Gradient norm is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning.
    HellaSwag accuracy is insensitive at 0.5B scale ($d < 1$ under QLoRA).
    Distinct-1 is non-monotonic, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
    Full fine-tuning produces sharper collapse onset ($15.3\times$ evaluation perplexity ratio at generation~1) than QLoRA ($8.7\times$) but lower terminal severity.
    These findings motivate a three-tier recommendation: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.
\end{enumerate}

Section~\ref{sec:related_work} surveys collapse theory, spectral analysis of neural networks, and concurrent monitoring approaches.
Section~\ref{sec:method} details our iterative contamination protocol, signal definitions, and evaluation framework.
Section~\ref{sec:results} presents signal--severity correlations, within-generation early warning analysis, and the method-dependent signal taxonomy.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses practical monitoring recommendations and limitations.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

% Introduction — collapse_severity_monitor
% Data sources: plan006 (3-seed Cohen's d), within_gen_analysis, plan003-fullft-05B

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

As LLM-generated text pervades web-scraped training corpora, practitioners increasingly fine-tune models on data shaped by prior model generations.
This recursive dynamic creates self-consuming loops that cause \emph{model collapse}---progressive loss of distribution tails, contraction of output diversity, and degradation of acquired knowledge~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
The problem compounds: even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse at sufficient depth~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors accumulating across iterations at accelerating rates~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}.
Yet the metrics practitioners most commonly watch during training fail to detect this degradation within a run.
Training perplexity can \emph{decrease} as a model collapses, since it measures fit to data that is itself partially synthetic.
Evaluation perplexity, computed on clean held-out data, reliably tracks severity \emph{across} generations but achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.534$ for within-generation collapse detection---indistinguishable from random chance.
A practitioner watching only perplexity would have no warning that collapse is underway until the next generation of synthetic data has already been produced.

Existing work addresses model collapse from two directions.
On the theoretical side, \citet{Shumailov2024} established the phenomenon, \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved that any nonzero synthetic fraction eventually induces strong collapse, and \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed that collapse alters neural scaling laws.
On the mitigation side, data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, and verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025} each reduce collapse pressure under specific conditions.
Missing from this landscape is a systematic analysis of which \emph{training-time signals} best track collapse severity, when they provide early warning, and where they saturate or actively mislead.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} highlight that even the definition of collapse varies across studies, further motivating signal-level analysis grounded in controlled experiments.
The two closest concurrent works---SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026}, which monitors output embedding spectra, and the topological index of \citet{Kalinowski2026}---each address part of this gap but carry limitations: SIGMA requires a clean reference distribution and operates post-hoc; topological monitoring incurs higher computational cost.
Neither provides a cross-family comparison of signal operating ranges or quantitative within-generation early warning thresholds.

We conduct a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as collapse severity monitors.
We evaluate four signal families---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (evaluation perplexity, token entropy, training loss), gradient (L2 norm), and downstream (HellaSwag accuracy)---across five experimental configurations spanning model scales (0.5B to 3B), fine-tuning methods (QLoRA and full fine-tuning), contamination fractions ($\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$), and text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed).
Our central finding is that different signal families have complementary operating ranges, and the same signal's utility can flip from informative to misleading depending on the training method.

Our contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Signal--severity correlation.}
    Spectral and output signals track collapse across contamination levels.
    Spectral entropy achieves the largest effect size (Cohen's $d = 33.48$, coefficient of variation $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
    Validated across QLoRA and full fine-tuning, six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change regardless of training method.
    The exception---gradient norm, which is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning---demonstrates that method-dependence is a first-order concern for monitoring pipeline design.

    \item \textbf{Within-generation early warning and negative results.}
    Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.984$ at 10\% training progress for binary collapse detection, with 34.4\% deviation from baseline at 3\% of training.
    Training loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$).
    We document two negative results: evaluation perplexity achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.534$ for within-generation detection---the most commonly available metric fails at the most actionable task---and token entropy achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$, providing no reliable discrimination despite a large initial deviation.
    These failures have a structural explanation: evaluation perplexity accumulates degradation through the iterative contamination loop, not within a single generation's training, while token entropy's per-position measurement lacks the representational sensitivity of spectral signals.

    \item \textbf{Signal taxonomy with method-dependent operating ranges.}
    Signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale.
    Gradient norm is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning.
    HellaSwag accuracy is insensitive at 0.5B scale ($d < 1$ under QLoRA).
    Distinct-1 is non-monotonic, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
    Full fine-tuning produces sharper collapse onset ($15.3\times$ evaluation perplexity ratio at generation~1) than QLoRA ($8.7\times$) but lower terminal severity.
    These findings motivate a three-tier recommendation: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.
\end{enumerate}

Section~\ref{sec:related_work} surveys collapse theory, spectral analysis of neural networks, and concurrent monitoring approaches.
Section~\ref{sec:method} details our iterative contamination protocol, signal definitions, and evaluation framework.
Section~\ref{sec:results} presents signal--severity correlations, within-generation early warning analysis, and the method-dependent signal taxonomy.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses practical monitoring recommendations and limitations.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

% Abstract — collapse_severity_monitor
% MVP evidence: mvp_frac50_100, within_gen_analysis, per_layer_analysis_v5
% Qwen2.5-0.5B, WikiText-2, QLoRA, 3 fractions (0/50/100%), seed 42, 5 generations

\begin{abstract}
Iterative training on synthetic data causes model collapse---progressive degradation in output quality and diversity---yet practitioners lack real-time tools to quantify its severity during training.
We systematically evaluate four families of training-time signals---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (token entropy, perplexity), gradient, and downstream---as collapse severity monitors across contamination levels and generational depth.
In controlled experiments (Qwen2.5-0.5B, WikiText-2, 5~iterative generations), spectral and output signals maintain monotonic severity ordering, with perplexity increasing $53\times$ and stable rank $6.6\times$ at full synthetic contamination.
Stable rank deviation reaches 34.4\% by 3\% of training progress, enabling early warning before catastrophic degradation materializes.
We document a signal taxonomy: spectral signals provide the earliest warning, output signals track severity most reliably, while gradient norms are non-monotonic under QLoRA and downstream benchmarks show minimal sensitivity at small scale.
Per-layer analysis reveals non-uniform collapse propagation, with specific sublayers exhibiting anomalous spectral signatures that diverge from aggregate-level trends.
These findings provide practitioners with actionable guidance for monitoring-based collapse detection during training.
\end{abstract}

% Conclusion section — collapse_severity_monitor
% Verified data sources: mvp_frac50_100, within_gen_analysis, per_layer_analysis_v5

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic empirical analysis of training dynamic signals as model collapse severity monitors.
Through controlled iterative retraining experiments on Qwen2.5-0.5B with WikiText-2 across three contamination levels and five generational depths, we established three main findings.
First, spectral signals (stable rank, spectral entropy) and output signals (token entropy, perplexity) maintain monotonic ordering with contamination severity, with effect sizes spanning orders of magnitude: $6.6\times$ stable rank separation and $53\times$ perplexity divergence at full contamination (source: \texttt{mvp\_frac50\_100}).
Second, stable rank deviation reaches 34.4\% at just 3\% of training progress, providing early warning before catastrophic degradation materializes (source: \texttt{within\_gen\_analysis}).
Third, not all signals are equally trustworthy: gradient norms are non-monotonic under QLoRA, downstream benchmarks are insensitive at small scale, and per-layer analysis reveals sub-module bifurcation invisible to aggregate metrics (source: \texttt{per\_layer\_analysis\_v5}).
Together, these findings yield a practitioner-oriented signal taxonomy that specifies which signals to trust, when, and at what granularity.

\paragraph{Broader impact.}
As LLM-generated text becomes increasingly prevalent in training corpora---through web scraping, synthetic data augmentation, and iterative self-improvement---the risk of undetected model collapse grows.
Our work contributes to AI safety by demonstrating that collapse leaves detectable fingerprints in standard training signals, well before it manifests in downstream benchmarks or human evaluation.
The monitoring signals we evaluate are computationally free (output signals) or near-free (spectral signals via periodic SVD), require no external reference distribution, and can be integrated into existing training pipelines with minimal engineering effort.
Making collapse visible during training---rather than discovering it post-hoc---enables practitioners to intervene before degradation becomes irreversible.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Several extensions would strengthen and broaden these findings.
%% TODO: plan_001 — 1.5B scale validation (in progress)
%% TODO: plan_002 — PubMed cross-domain validation (in progress)
%% TODO: plan_003 — Full FT comparison
First, scale and domain validation: confirming that signal--severity correlations hold at scales of practical interest ($\geq$7B) and across diverse text domains would establish generalizability.
Second, monitoring-to-intervention: translating early warning signals into automated intervention triggers---adaptive learning rate reduction, selective data filtering, or training rollback when spectral deviation exceeds calibrated thresholds---would close the loop from detection to mitigation.
Third, broader collapse sources: evaluating signal behavior under distribution shift, data poisoning, and mixed-provenance synthetic data would test whether our taxonomy generalizes beyond the iterative self-generation setting.
Finally, a lightweight, open-source monitoring toolkit that computes the recommended signals as a standard training callback would lower the adoption barrier for practitioners, enabling collapse-aware training as a default practice rather than a research exercise.

% Results section — collapse_severity_monitor
% Data sources: plan006 (3-seed Cohen's d), within_gen_analysis, plan003-fullft-05B, heatmap_data.json

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We organize results around three claims.
Section~\ref{sec:correlation} establishes that spectral and output signals track collapse severity across configurations.
Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results} shows that certain signals detect collapse within a single training run before evaluation perplexity diverges.
Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy} reveals that signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method, motivating a taxonomy of method-dependent operating ranges.

\subsection{Signal--Severity Correlation}
\label{sec:correlation}

We quantify signal sensitivity using Cohen's $d$ between the clean baseline ($\alpha = 0$) and full contamination ($\alpha = 1.0$) at generation~4, computed across three seeds (C1 configuration; Table~\ref{tab:configs}).
Effect sizes, rather than rank correlations, serve as the primary evidence because they convey the magnitude of signal separation, not just its ordering.

\paragraph{Effect sizes.}
Spectral entropy achieves the largest and most reproducible effect size ($d = 33.48$, coefficient of variation across seeds $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$), distinct-1 ($d = 14.60$), and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
Distinct-2 ($d = 7.59$) and distinct-3 ($d = -7.08$; negative because collapse increases trigram repetition) provide moderate separation.
Token entropy, self-BLEU, gradient norm, and HellaSwag accuracy yield small effect sizes ($d < 5$), placing them in a second tier for cross-generation severity discrimination (Figure~\ref{fig:severity_curves}).

Stable rank warrants a cautionary note on seed sensitivity.
With two seeds, $d = 61.7$; adding a third seed reduced this to $d = 9.43$---a rank change from 1st to 4th among monitored signals.
Its $\mathrm{CV}$ of 0.022 is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's 0.0015.
We treat stable rank as informative but seed-sensitive at this sample size; $N = 3$ seeds are insufficient for a Wilcoxon test (minimum $p = 0.25$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals for inference.

% TODO: 1.5B × 5-seed bootstrap CI pending (C2 configuration). Will provide tighter effect size estimates and enable rank stability analysis.
% TODO: PubMed cross-domain replication (C3 configuration) in progress.

\paragraph{Cross-method consistency.}
Six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change under both QLoRA and full fine-tuning (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}): spectral entropy, stable rank, evaluation perplexity, token entropy, distinct-1, and self-BLEU all move in the same direction as contamination increases, regardless of training method.
The exception is gradient norm, which exhibits non-monotonic behavior under QLoRA but monotonic decrease under full fine-tuning (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

\paragraph{Supporting rank correlations.}
Spearman correlations provide directional confirmation: spectral entropy maintains high $|\rho|$ across generations.
However, $|\rho| = 1.0$ for stable rank across contamination fractions is trivially achieved with few contamination levels and should not be interpreted as strong evidence of monotonicity.
We therefore use Cohen's $d$ as the primary sensitivity measure throughout.


\subsection{Within-Generation Early Warning}
\label{sec:early_warning_results}

Cross-generation tracking (Section~\ref{sec:correlation}) requires completing multiple generations to assess severity.
A more actionable capability is detecting collapse \emph{within} a single training run, enabling early stopping before degradation accumulates.
We evaluate this using the relative deviation $\Delta_s$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:deviation}) and AUROC for binary collapse detection at each checkpoint.

\paragraph{Stable rank as early alarm.}
At 10\% training progress, stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.984$ for distinguishing $\alpha = 1.0$ from $\alpha = 0$ (Figure~\ref{fig:roc_curves}; Table~\ref{tab:within_gen_roc}).
At step~50 (3\% of training), $\Delta_\mathrm{SR} = 34.4\%$---far exceeding the 5\% detection threshold defined in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}.
Stable rank's within-generation sensitivity reflects the structural nature of spectral signals: contamination alters the covariance eigenspectrum before output-level metrics respond, because energy dispersal across representation dimensions (Eq.~\ref{eq:stable_rank}) is detectable even when the model's token-level predictions have not yet degraded.

% TODO: Figure~\ref{fig:roc_curves} uses synthetic ROC curves generated from known AUC values. Replace with empirical ROC data from plan001 5-seed validation.

\paragraph{Spectral and token entropy.}
Token entropy deviates 24.5\% at step~50 but achieves only $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$ at 10\% progress---near random chance, indicating that despite its large initial deviation, token entropy provides no reliable within-generation discrimination.
Spectral entropy achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.773$, providing moderate within-generation discrimination but still substantially below stable rank's 0.984.

\paragraph{Evaluation perplexity fails within-generation detection.}
Evaluation perplexity achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.534$ at 10\% training progress---indistinguishable from random.
This failure has a clear mechanistic explanation.
Training perplexity measures fit to the current (potentially contaminated) data mix and can \emph{decrease} under collapse because the model fits its own synthetic output.
Evaluation perplexity, computed on clean held-out data, does track degradation in language modeling quality---but this degradation accumulates \emph{across} generations through the iterative contamination loop (Eq.~\ref{eq:mixing}), not within a single generation's training run.
Within one generation, the model trains on a fixed corpus $\mathcal{D}_g$; it has not yet produced the synthetic data that will contaminate $\mathcal{D}_{g+1}$.
Consequently, evaluation perplexity does not diverge from baseline within a single run, even when collapse is underway.

Spectral signals, by contrast, detect structural change---the dispersal of representational energy across dimensions---independent of whether the model's next-token predictions have degraded on held-out text.
This structural sensitivity explains stable rank's near-perfect within-generation discrimination at a checkpoint where perplexity-based detection is no better than chance.

% TODO: Within-gen ROC results are from N=1 seed at 0.5B (C1). Pending plan001 5-seed validation at 1.5B to determine AUC stability.


\subsection{Signal Taxonomy: Method-Dependent Operating Ranges}
\label{sec:taxonomy}

The cross-method comparison (C1 vs C4; Table~\ref{tab:configs}) reveals that the same signal can be informative under one training method and misleading under another.

\paragraph{Gradient norm: method-dependent.}
Under QLoRA, gradient norm changes non-monotonically with contamination: $+5.9\%$ at $\alpha = 0.5$ relative to baseline, then $-30.8\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$.
Under full fine-tuning, gradient norm decreases monotonically ($-58.3\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$), consistent with the model converging more easily to lower-entropy synthetic data.
The QLoRA non-monotonicity likely arises from the interaction between contaminated gradients and the rank-$r$ adapter subspace~\citep{hu2022lora}: at moderate contamination, gradients from mixed real/synthetic data create conflicting update directions within the low-rank projection, inflating the norm; at full contamination, the uniform synthetic signal reduces this conflict~\citep{dettmers2023qlora}.
This method-dependence means gradient norm cannot be used as a collapse indicator without knowing the training configuration (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}).

\paragraph{Downstream and diversity metrics: insensitive at 0.5B.}
HellaSwag accuracy is insensitive under QLoRA ($-1.15\%$, $d < 1$).
Under full fine-tuning, the $\alpha = 0$ baseline is unavailable, preventing direct effect size computation; the available data show accuracy of $0.397$ ($\alpha = 0.5$) and $0.372$ ($\alpha = 1.0$), a $-6.3\%$ relative change between these two conditions.

Distinct-1 is non-monotonic under QLoRA: $+17.7\%$ at $\alpha = 0.5$ but $-12.5\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
Self-BLEU is insensitive to collapse even when evaluation perplexity increases $17\times$.
This disconnect arises because nucleus sampling ($p = 0.95$) draws from the distribution tail, producing superficially diverse surface forms even as the model's probability mass concentrates on fewer modes.
Token entropy captures this concentration (Section~\ref{sec:correlation}), but $n$-gram diversity metrics do not.
Monitoring pipelines that rely solely on output diversity metrics risk missing collapse entirely.

\paragraph{Full fine-tuning collapse dynamics.}
Full fine-tuning produces sharper onset but lower terminal severity than QLoRA (Figure~\ref{fig:method_comparison}).
The generation~0 to generation~1 evaluation perplexity ratio is $15.3\times$ under full FT versus $8.7\times$ under QLoRA.
However, post-onset growth saturates rapidly: the generation~1 to generation~4 ratio is $1.11\times$ under full FT, compared to continued growth under QLoRA.
Terminal severity at generation~4 is lower: full FT reaches $\mathrm{PPL}_\text{eval} = 326.19$ versus QLoRA's $839.2$ ($0.39\times$).
This pattern---fast onset, early saturation---is consistent with full parameter access enabling rapid adaptation to synthetic data characteristics, followed by convergence to a lower-entropy attractor.

We observe that terminal stable rank values are similar across methods: $\mathrm{SR} = 153.87$ (full FT) versus $155.64$ (QLoRA) at generation~4, $\alpha = 1.0$.
This comparison rests on $N = 1$ seed per method and cannot be distinguished from coincidence; we note it as an observation, not a finding.

\paragraph{Recommended operating ranges.}
Based on the evidence above, we propose signal-to-task assignments (Table~\ref{tab:signal_taxonomy}):
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Within-generation alarm:} stable rank ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.984$ at 10\% training progress).
    \item \textbf{Cross-generation severity discrimination:} spectral entropy ($d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$).
    \item \textbf{Cross-generation tracking:} evaluation perplexity (large absolute effect, interpretable scale).
    \item \textbf{Method-dependent:} gradient norm (monotonic under full FT only).
    \item \textbf{Non-monotonic:} distinct-1 ($+17.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.5$, $-12.5\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$ under QLoRA).
    \item \textbf{Insensitive at 0.5B scale:} HellaSwag accuracy ($d < 1$).
\end{itemize}

\noindent
These assignments are derived from 0.5B models on WikiText-2 with $N \leq 3$ seeds.
The full FT comparison uses $N = 1$ seed.
Validation across larger models, additional domains, and larger seed counts is required before these operating ranges can be considered robust.

import json
import os

    'font.family': 'DejaVu Sans',
    'font.size': 11,
    'axes.titlesize': 13,

})

C_FT = '#E69F00'
C_QL = '#0072B2'

script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
with open(os.path.join(script_dir, 'comparison_data.json')) as f:
    data = json.load(f)

ft_traj = data['fullft_trajectories']['100pct']
ql_traj = data['qlora_trajectories']['100pct']

ft_ppl = ft_traj['ppl']
ft_hella = ft_traj['hellaswag']
ql_ppl = ql_traj['ppl']
ql_hella = ql_traj['hellaswag']

gens = np.arange(len(ft_ppl))

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.75, 3.4))

# --- Panel (a): Perplexity ---
ax1.plot(gens, ft_ppl, 'o-', color=C_FT, label='Full FT (100%)', markersize=5, zorder=3)
ax1.plot(gens, ql_ppl, 'o-', color=C_QL, label='QLoRA (100%)', markersize=5, zorder=3)
ax1.set_yscale('log')
ax1.set_xlabel('Generation')
ax1.set_ylabel('Perplexity')
ax1.set_title('(a) Perplexity')
ax1.set_xticks(gens)

onset_ft = ft_ppl[1] / ft_ppl[0]

ax1.annotate(f'{onset_ft:.1f}×', xy=(0.5, mid_y_ft), fontsize=9, fontweight='bold',
             color=C_FT, ha='center', va='bottom',

onset_ql = ql_ppl[1] / ql_ppl[0]

ax1.annotate(f'{onset_ql:.1f}×', xy=(0.5, mid_y_ql), fontsize=9, fontweight='bold',
             color=C_QL, ha='center', va='top',
             bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.2', fc='white', ec=C_QL, alpha=0.85, lw=0.8))

ax1.legend(loc='lower right', framealpha=0.9)

# --- Panel (b): HellaSwag ---

if ft_hella_valid:
    ft_hx, ft_hy = zip(*ft_hella_valid)
    ax2.plot(ft_hx, ft_hy, 'o-', color=C_FT, label='Full FT (100%)', markersize=5, zorder=3)
if ql_hella_valid:
    ql_hx, ql_hy = zip(*ql_hella_valid)

ax2.set_xlabel('Generation')
ax2.set_ylabel('HellaSwag Accuracy')
ax2.set_title('(b) HellaSwag Accuracy')
ax2.set_xticks(gens)
ax2.set_xticklabels([f'gen{i}' for i in gens])
ax2.set_ylim(0.35, 0.46)
ax2.legend(loc='lower left', framealpha=0.9)

plt.tight_layout(w_pad=2.5)

out_dir = script_dir
fig.savefig(os.path.join(out_dir, 'fig5_method_comparison.pdf'))
fig.savefig(os.path.join(out_dir, 'fig5_method_comparison.png'))
plt.close()

print("=== Data verification ===")
print(f"Full FT PPL:      {ft_ppl}")
print(f"Full FT HellaSwag: {ft_hella}")
print(f"QLoRA PPL:        {ql_ppl}")
print(f"QLoRA HellaSwag:  {ql_hella}")

print(f"QL onset ratio:   {onset_ql:.2f}x")

for ext in ['pdf', 'png']:
